title: Synaptic Pruning Over a Lifetime
description: Interactive simulation with an age slider from birth to 30 years. Two small neural network patches (sensory cortex and prefrontal cortex) gain and then lose synapses while long-range axons gain myelin, and a schematic graph shows relative synapse density in each region and relative white matter volume. Sensory cortex peaks and prunes early; prefrontal cortex peaks later and keeps pruning into the twenties; white matter keeps rising into the late twenties.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
Brain Development
Synaptic Pruning
Myelination
Adolescent Brain
learningObjectives: Compare the timing of synapse overproduction and pruning in sensory cortex versus prefrontal cortex from birth to age 30.
Explain why continued prefrontal pruning and myelination mean brain development continues through adolescence and into the twenties, without a single fixed end age.
prerequisites: Location and role of the prefrontal cortex (Chapter 4)
keyQuestions: Which region reaches its peak synapse density first?
At age 16, which region is still pruning synapses?
Why can removing synapses make brain circuits work better?
Why is it misleading to say the brain finishes developing at exactly 25?
misconceptions: More synapses always means a better brain.
The whole brain develops on the same schedule.
Brain development stops at a single age, such as 18 or 25.
The schematic curves show exact synapse counts.
controls: Start/Pause button: plays the age forward automatically from birth to 30, then loops
Age slider: sets age from 0 to 30 years in steps of 0.1
